title: Replication — master-slave (read replicas), master-master (conflict resolution needed), replication lag, failover.

s1_definition.profdef: Replication copies data from one database to one or more others to improve read scalability, availability, and durability. In master-slave replication, a single primary accepts writes and replicates to read-only replicas that serve reads. In master-master replication, multiple nodes accept writes and must resolve conflicts. Replication lag is the delay before a replica reflects a write, and failover is the process of promoting a replica to primary when the primary fails.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India keeps one official master ledger where all changes are written, and several photocopies that tellers across branches read from so they do not crowd the master. The copies lag the master by a tiny moment. If the master ledger is destroyed, one photocopy is promoted to become the new official master. If instead two branches could both write to their own copies, they might record conflicting changes to the same account, and the bank would need rules to reconcile them. That whole copying arrangement is replication.
s1_definition.oneliner: Copy data to replicas for read scale and availability; master-slave has one writer, master-master has many writers needing conflict resolution, replicas lag, and failover promotes a replica when the primary dies.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Replication copies data from one database to one or more others to improve read scalability, availability, and durability. In master-slave replication, a single primary accepts writes and replicates to read-only replicas that serve reads. In master-master replication, multiple nodes accept writes and must resolve conflicts. Replication lag is the delay before a replica reflects a write, and failover is the process of promoting a replica to primary when the primary fails.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India keeps one official master ledger where all changes are written, and several photocopies that tellers across branches read from so they do not crowd the master. The copies lag the master by a tiny moment. If the master ledger is destroyed, one photocopy is promoted to become the new official master. If instead two branches could both write to their own copies, they might record conflicting changes to the same account, and the bank would need rules to reconcile them. That whole copying arrangement is replication.

**One line to remember:** Copy data to replicas for read scale and availability; master-slave has one writer, master-master has many writers needing conflict resolution, replicas lag, and failover promotes a replica when the primary dies.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's single database is overwhelmed by read traffic from millions of balance and statement checks, slowing down the writes that actually move money. The real problem is read load crowding out writes. This is exactly what master-slave read replicas solve.

Problem 2 — right after Rajesh transfers money, he refreshes and must see his new balance, but a lagging replica might show the old one. The real problem is read-your-own-writes under replication lag. This is exactly what routing a just-written user's read to the primary solves.

Problem 3 — the primary database crashes, and the bank must keep operating by promoting a replica without two nodes both accepting writes. The real problem is safe failover without split-brain. This is exactly what failover with fencing handles.

We build a runnable replication core: a `Primary`, several `Replica` instances with simulated lag, a `ReplicationManager` routing writes and reads with read-your-writes handling, and a `Failover` that promotes a replica and fences the old primary. The demo scales reads across replicas, handles lag for a just-written user, and promotes a replica on primary failure.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is one primary and two replicas, a balance write, reads before and after replication, a read-your-writes read, and a primary failure.

Step 1: The balance write goes only to the primary, which applies it and queues the change for replication. Reading the primary immediately shows the new value.

Step 2: A replica read before replication completes shows the stale or absent value, demonstrating replication lag: the replica has not yet received the change.

Step 3: Replication runs, applying the queued change to both replicas, after which a replica read shows the consistent new value. This is how reads are scaled across replicas once they catch up.

Step 4: A read-your-writes read for a user who just wrote is routed to the primary, so they always see their own change immediately regardless of lag. Then the primary crashes; failover promotes a replica to primary and fences the old primary so it cannot accept writes and cause split-brain. A new write succeeds on the promoted primary. The data that changed is the primary role moving to a replica and writes continuing on the new primary.

```
2026-11-01 01:50:00 [INFO] WRITE to primary balance:SAV2001=950000
2026-11-01 01:50:00 [INFO] primary balance = 950000
2026-11-01 01:50:00 [INFO] replica read (may lag) = <absent>
2026-11-01 01:50:00 [INFO] replicas caught up
2026-11-01 01:50:00 [INFO] replica read after replicate = 950000
2026-11-01 01:50:00 [WARNING] promoted replica-1; fenced primary
2026-11-01 01:50:00 [INFO] after failover, new primary balance = 930000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  WRITE balance:SAV2001=950000
    │ only to PRIMARY
    ▼
  primary applies + queues change
    │
    ├─ read primary → 950000 (immediate)
    ├─ read replica BEFORE replicate → <absent>  (LAG)
    │
    │ replicate() → apply to replica-1, replica-2
    ▼
  read replica AFTER → 950000 (consistent)

  read-your-writes (justWrote=true) → PRIMARY → always fresh

  PRIMARY CRASH
    │ Failover.promote
    │  fence old primary (no split-brain)
    │  replica-1 → new PRIMARY
    ▼
  new writes accepted on replica-1
```

  [REPLICA] ──promote──→ [PRIMARY] ──crash──→ [FENCED]
      ▲                                           │

  ── Call Chain (write + failover) ──────────────────────────

  1. mgr.write(key, value) → primary.apply + queue
  2. mgr.replicate() → replicas apply queued changes
  3. mgr.read(key, justWrote=true) → primary (read-your-writes)

  5. mgr.write(...) → new primary accepts

    Pre:  primary not fenced
    Post: applied to primary, queued for replicas
    Reads lag on replicas until replicate(); recent writer reads primary

sections.s6_takeaway:
Replication copies data from one database to others to improve read scalability, availability, and durability, and the pattern I reach for first in banking is master-slave. A single primary accepts all writes and streams its change log to read-only replicas, and I spread reads across those replicas. This fits banking perfectly because the traffic is overwhelmingly reads, like balance checks and statements, and keeping a single writer makes the writes that actually move money simple and consistent. At National Bank of India, this stopped read traffic from crowding out the money-moving writes.

The reality I always address is replication lag, the delay before a write on the primary appears on a replica. With asynchronous replication the write is acknowledged as soon as the primary commits, which is fast but means a replica can be briefly behind, causing a read-your-own-writes anomaly where a customer does not immediately see their own change on a lagging replica. I handle this by routing a user's read to the primary right after they write, so Rajesh always sees his new balance immediately even while replicas catch up. Semi-synchronous replication, which waits for at least one replica to acknowledge, is a middle ground that trades a little write latency for stronger durability.

Master-master replication, where multiple nodes accept writes, improves write availability and locality but introduces conflicts when two nodes modify the same row concurrently. Those conflicts must be resolved by strategies like last-write-wins, which can silently lose data, or application-specific merging. For money this is dangerous, because conflicting balance writes are unacceptable, so a bank almost always keeps a single writer per piece of data rather than true master-master on financial records.

Failover is the final piece: when the primary fails, the system must detect it, promote the most up-to-date replica, redirect writes, and fence off the old primary so it cannot resume and create split-brain, where two nodes both believe they are primary. In the demo, the promoted replica took over and the old primary was fenced, so new writes continued safely. The senior trade-off I always name is that asynchronous replication risks losing recently acknowledged writes during failover, while synchronous replication protects them at the cost of latency, and for a bank I resolve that trade-off toward durability, because losing an acknowledged transaction is far worse than a slightly slower write.
